details:
Ridgeline is an offline map for astronauts walking on Mars. It covers a real 6 km site on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater and answers the four questions every Mars walk raises: Where can I safely walk? Which stops are worth the trip? Where am I without GPS? Where do I go when a storm comes?

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

- Plan the walk: Ridgeline builds walking routes on a 10 m terrain model of the site. Ground steeper than 25° is ruled out. Walking time uses a standard hiking-speed model, adjusted for a pressure suit and the load carried. Every route shows how much spare air is left at the tightest stop and when to turn back. Users can add their own stops, and the times update instantly.

- Choose science stops: Stops are ranked by science value, for example the boxwork ridge textures Curiosity is studying. Users can switch between satellite, terrain and slope maps.

- Find my position without GPS: Mars has no GPS, so the estimated position drifts as the crew walks, and the map shows how far off it could be. Pressing "Find my position" matches the horizon the astronaut sees against 13,000 skylines precomputed from the terrain. The median error in our tests is 11 m.

- Storm warning: A modelled solar storm, based on Curiosity's May 2024 radiation reading, warns the crew up to 30 minutes ahead. It shows the nearest cover and whether they can reach it in time.

- Helmet view: A 3D first-person view shows the walk at eye level, with the route, stops and storm alerts in place.

- Proof: A page tests our numbers against Curiosity's real drives. All of the rover's path inside the site lies on ground we mark walkable, and our routes are a median 0.96 times the length of the rover's drives. Every made-up value is labelled as an assumption on the page.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Future crews will walk where there is no GPS, no live help from Earth and little margin for error. Ridgeline shows how real NASA orbital and rover data can become a tool a crew can trust. It runs fully offline, explains its uncertainty instead of hiding it, and puts safety (air, slope, radiation) first. It also works as a teaching tool: anyone can explore Mount Sharp and see why planning a Mars walk is hard.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Data: NASA and USGS data: HiRISE and CTX stereo terrain and imagery (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter); MOLA (Mars Global Surveyor) and HRSC (Mars Express) regional terrain; Curiosity's rover localization, plus its RAD radiation and REMS weather data.

- Data processing: Python pipelines using NumPy and SciPy, with uv for packages. Tests run on pytest and ruff.

- Web app: TypeScript and React 19, built with Vite. MapLibre for maps, three.js and React Three Fiber for 3D, Zustand for app state, Tailwind CSS for styling. Works offline as an installable PWA. Tested with Vitest.

- Hardware: Our own laptops. Ridgeline runs in any browser on a phone, tablet or desktop, with a light theme for projectors.

HOW IT'S CREATIVE

Most Mars maps are for looking at. Ridgeline is for walking. Finding your position by matching the skyline is the way a human navigator would orient on Mars. The storm warning tells you where to go, not just that danger is coming. And the app checks itself against the real rover's drives, so it doesn't ask to be trusted blindly.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Astronaut safety: suit speed, carried load, air reserve, slope limits and radiation exposure.

- No connectivity: everything works offline, with no live calls to NASA.

- Honesty: every estimate shows its uncertainty, and every assumption is labelled in the app.

- Usability under pressure: large, clear numbers, a guided demo, and layouts that work on every screen size.

- Accuracy: distances, slopes and positions are all computed on real terrain at true height.
